stem: A lessee's office lease bundles rent, common area maintenance, and a front-desk service contract into one monthly payment. Under ASC 842's default requirements, how does the lessee account for the payment?

choices.text: Separate the lease component from the nonlease components and allocate the payment on relative standalone prices
Treat the whole payment as a lease payment, since the contract is called a lease
Expense the whole payment as rent, since the components cannot be observed separately
Capitalize the whole payment as part of the right-of-use asset

feedback: By default, the lease component — the right to use the space — is separated from the nonlease components — the maintenance and services — and the consideration is allocated across them in proportion to standalone prices, with estimates where observable standalone prices are not readily available. Answer (b) describes the elected treatment of 842-10-15-37, not the default; (c) gives up on an allocation the standard requires the lessee to make or estimate; (d) confuses the asset with the payment stream. Re-study block 2 (S-02, the default).
_source: ASC 842-10-15-31 (default separation) and 842-10-15-33(a)-(b) (relative standalone price allocation; estimation where observable prices are not readily available), as issued in sources/asc842/ASU_2016-02_Section_A.pdf pp. 19-20; sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt for the election that switches the default off

stem: How does a lessee make the election in 842-10-15-37 not to separate nonlease components?

choices.text: As an accounting policy election by class of underlying asset, covering each lease component and its associated nonlease components
Contract by contract, whenever separation would be inconvenient
Entity-wide, for every lease of every asset class at once
By notifying the lessor that the components will be combined

feedback: The paragraph's own words: 'as an accounting policy election by class of underlying asset,' combining each separate lease component with the nonlease components associated with that lease component. Answer (b) is the lease-by-lease convenience reading that a policy election forbids; (c) overshoots the boundary — the class, not the entity, is the unit of election; (d) invents a counterparty step — this is the lessee's accounting policy, and the lessor's own election is separate. Re-study block 3 (S-03, the election).

stem: A lessee elects not to separate nonlease components for its real estate class. Compared with separating, what happens to its financial statements?

choices.text: The lease liability and right-of-use asset are larger; total expense over the term is unchanged
Total expense over the term increases, because service costs are now lease costs
Nothing changes — the election is presentation only
The lease liability shrinks, because the components are no longer priced separately

feedback: Electing makes the whole payment a lease payment, so the liability and the matching right-of-use asset grow by the present value of the nonlease money — dollars that would otherwise never touch the balance sheet. What the election cannot do is change what the lessee pays: total expense over the term is the total consideration either way. Answer (b) double-counts — the service dollars change caption, not amount; (c) understates a real balance-sheet change; (d) runs the effect backwards. Re-study block 4 (S-04, what electing does).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt (single lease component); sources/asc842/842-20-25-6.txt item (a) (single straight-line lease cost); see drafts/ASC842-PCX-03-review.md on the expense-pattern caveat

stem: A landlord and tenant sign the same bundled office lease. The tenant elects not to separate nonlease components. Does the landlord's accounting follow?

choices.text: No — the election is written for the lessee, and the lessor allocates the consideration under its own requirements
Yes — the components of one contract must be classified the same way by both parties
Yes — the lessee's election binds the lessor once disclosed
No — but only because the landlord did not consent to the tenant's election

feedback: The election in 842-10-15-37 is written for a lessee — 'a lessee may, as an accounting policy election' — and nothing in it reaches the other side of the contract: the lessor allocates the consideration to the lease and nonlease components under its own requirements, which 842-10-15-38 takes from the revenue standard. So the two sides of one contract can properly account for it differently. Answers (b) and (c) assume a symmetry the standard does not impose; (d) reaches the right answer by an invented mechanism — the election is a unilateral accounting policy, not something a counterparty consents to. Re-study block 6 (S-06, the lessor caution).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt ('a lessee may'); ASC 842-10-15-38 (lessor allocation under Topic 606), as issued in sources/asc842/ASU_2016-02_Section_A.pdf p. 20

stem: In the worked example — $6,000 bundled monthly payment, $5,000 space and $1,000 services, three years — electing the single-lease-component treatment changed which figure?

choices.text: The initial lease liability and right-of-use asset, which grew by roughly $33,400
Total expense over the term, which grew by $36,000
The monthly cash payment to the landlord
Nothing — both treatments produce identical statements

feedback: Electing moved the present value of the $1,000 service stream onto the balance sheet — about $33,400 more liability and the same again in right-of-use asset — while profit and loss carried $6,000 a month and $216,000 over the term under either treatment. Answer (b) mistakes the balance-sheet gross-up for extra expense; (c) confuses accounting treatment with the contract — cash never changes; (d) forgets the statements differ exactly where the liability lives. Re-study block 7 (S-07, the worked example).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt; figures are illustrative arithmetic — see drafts/ASC842-PCX-03-review.md

stem: A bundled monthly payment on a leased clinic building covers the building itself, janitorial services, and a security-monitoring contract. Under ASC 842, which parts are nonlease components?

choices.text: The janitorial services and the security monitoring
The building — services are what the contract is really for
All three — a bundled contract has no lease component
None — everything in a lease contract is a lease component

feedback: The lease component is the right to use the identified asset — the building. Janitorial and monitoring services are things the supplier does rather than assets whose use the customer controls, which makes them nonlease components: separated and allocated by default, or folded into the lease component only under an 842-10-15-37 election. Answer (b) inverts the analysis; (c) throws out a lease that plainly exists; (d) is the assumption the default separation requirement exists to correct. Re-study block 1 (S-01, what the payment buys).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt (lease vs nonlease components); ASC 842-10-15-3 (a lease conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset), as issued in sources/asc842/ASU_2016-02_Section_A.pdf p. 13 and reproduced unamended in sources/asc842/ASU_2023-01.txt

stem: A lessee has elected 842-10-15-37 for its vehicle class. It leases a delivery van under a contract that bundles the van with a maintenance plan. How does it account for the contract?

choices.text: As a single lease component: the van lease and its associated maintenance together
As a lease of the van plus a separately allocated maintenance expense
It may choose either treatment for this van, contract by contract
As a service contract, since maintenance is included

feedback: Within an elected class, the election is the policy: each separate lease component and the nonlease components associated with it are accounted for as a single lease component — so the van and its maintenance plan become one lease. Answer (b) describes the default the election switched off for this class; (c) reintroduces contract-by-contract discretion that an accounting policy election removes; (d) lets the service tail wag the lease dog — bundling maintenance does not un-lease the van. Re-study block 3 (S-03, the election).

stem: Which statement correctly describes the financial statement effect of a lessee's election not to separate nonlease components?

choices.text: The lease liability includes the nonlease payments, so the balance sheet grows while total expense over the term does not change
The income statement grows, because service costs are recognized twice
The balance sheet shrinks, because one component is smaller than several
Only disclosures change; recognition and measurement are unaffected

feedback: Folding nonlease payments into the lease payment enlarges the present value that becomes the lease liability and right-of-use asset; the payments themselves — and therefore total expense over the term — are what they always were. Answer (b) invents double-counting that no treatment produces; (c) reasons from the word 'single' instead of from the payments being combined; (d) understates an election that changes initial measurement of both sides of the balance sheet. Re-study blocks 4 and 7 (S-04 and S-07).

stem: For which asset class is the election not to separate nonlease components most likely to be cost-effective for a lessee?

choices.text: A class where nonlease services are a small slice of each payment and standalone prices would have to be estimated
A class where bundled service components make up most of each payment
Any class, since the election never affects the balance sheet
A class where the lessor consents to combining the components

feedback: The election trades a larger liability for the end of the allocation work, so it pays best where the liability cost is trivial — services a sliver of the payment — and the allocation cost is real, as when standalone prices must be estimated. Answer (b) picks the class where electing would put the most service money on the balance sheet as a debt-like liability, the case for keeping separation; (c) forgets the liability grows at all; (d) invents a counterparty condition — the election is the lessee's own accounting policy, and the lessor's allocation is governed by the lessor's own requirements. Re-study block 5 (S-05, when to elect).
_source: sources/asc842/842-10-15-37.txt (by-class election); the cost-benefit reasoning is application — see drafts/ASC842-PCX-03-review.md
